title: Navigating the Latent Space Dynamics of Neural Models
claim: Autoencoders implicitly define latent vector fields whose attractors align with high-density regions of the data, regardless of initialization.
layout: 5 panels in a row, same axes, differing initializations, viridis colormap
description: A single horizontal strip of five square quiver-style plots. Each plot shows the 2-D latent vector field of an autoencoder with bottleneck size 2, trained on MNIST. The axes run from -8 to 8. Each panel comes from a different random initialization. Arrows are colored with the viridis colormap by vector norm. Violet means a small norm and yellow means a large norm. Near the edges, long arrows radiate outward in teal, green and yellow. Their length is greatest along bright diagonal streaks. In the center, a flower-like or blob-like white region marks where the field vanishes. This is the latent manifold's support, where attractors sit. Its shape differs across the five panels, but each has the same overall character. The eye goes first to the bright white central blobs against the dark violet and teal surroundings. There are no labels or arrows between panels.
caption: Latent dynamics of AEs. Latent vector fields induced by autoencoders with bottleneck $k=2$, trained on MNIST, with $z_0 \sim \mathcal{U}[-8,8]$. Models with different initializations are shown. Colors (viridis colormap) represent vector norms ranging from violet (low) to yellow (high). The shape of the latent manifold identifies with the encoder's support. White regions indicate where the vector field vanishes, revealing attractors aligned with high-density areas of the data distribution.
abstract: Neural networks transform high-dimensional data into compact, structured representations, often modeled as elements of a lower dimensional latent space. In this paper, we present an alternative interpretation of neural models as dynamical systems acting on the latent manifold. Specifically, we show that autoencoder models implicitly define a latent vector field on the manifold, derived by iteratively applying the encoding-decoding map, without any additional training. We observe that standard training procedures introduce inductive biases that lead to the emergence of attractor points within this vector field. Drawing on this insight, we propose to leverage the vector field as a representation for the network, providing a novel tool to analyze the properties of the model and the data. This representation enables to: (i) analyze the generalization and memorization regimes of neural models, even throughout training; (ii) extract prior knowledge encoded in the network's parameters from the attractors, without requiring any input data; (iii) identify out-of-distribution samples from their trajectories in the vector field. We further validate our approach on vision foundation models, showcasing the applicability and effectiveness of our method in real-world scenarios.
